explain: NER finds mentions of entities in text (person names, organizations, places, dates, amounts) and assigns each one the correct category.
options: Translating a text from a source language to a different target language, as in machine translation
Finding mentions of entities in text and assigning them a category such as PERSON, ORGANIZATION, or LOCATION
Summarizing a long document by condensing its main points into new sentences, as in abstractive summarization
Generating new paragraphs coherent with a given context, as a language generation model does
q: Which of the following activities best describes the Named Entity Recognition (NER) task?

explain: B marks the beginning of an entity, I marks internal continuation tokens, and O indicates tokens outside any entity.
options: Beginning, Inside, Outside: entity start, continuation, and tokens outside any entity
Binary Input Output: binary encoding of the textual input and the model output
Beginning Input Output: marker for neural network input start and output end
Begin Intermediate Other: start, intermediate token, and residual category for everything else
q: In the BIO/IOB labeling scheme for NER, what do the letters B, I, and O mean?

explain: Sentiment analysis classifies the opinion expressed in a text, typically as positive, negative, or neutral.
options: Topic classification: assigning a text the thematic category it deals with, such as sports or politics
Intent classification: recognizing the goal or action requested by the user in a dialogue
Sentiment analysis: classifying the polarity of the expressed opinion, such as positive or negative
Coreference resolution: establishing which different mentions refer to the same entity
q: A company wants to automatically classify customer reviews as positive, negative, or neutral. What is this task called?

explain: Intent classification understands the user's goal (booking, canceling, asking for info) and is the heart of chatbots and virtual assistants.
options: Sentiment analysis: classifying the emotional polarity of the message as positive or negative
Topic classification: assigning the message the topic it deals with, such as travel or restaurants
Named Entity Recognition: finding and classifying names of people, places, and organizations in the text
Intent classification: mapping the utterance to the user's goal, here the book_flight action
q: In a chatbot, the sentence 'I want to book a flight to Rome' must be mapped to the action book_flight. Which task is this?

explain: Topic classification assigns a text the topic it talks about, such as sports, politics, or technology.
options: Sentiment analysis: assessing whether the text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral opinion
Topic classification: assigning each article the thematic section it deals with, such as sports
Extractive question answering: extracting from each article the exact span that answers a given question
Machine translation: automatically translating each article into another target language
q: Automatically sorting newspaper articles into sections such as sports, politics, and technology is an example of:

explain: Tokenization splits text into units (words, subwords, or characters) and converts them into numeric IDs; modern models use subword tokenizers such as BPE or WordPiece.
options: Splitting text into smaller units (words or subwords) mapped to numeric IDs
Encrypting text with cryptographic algorithms to protect its confidentiality
Removing stopwords from text, i.e., common words considered uninformative
Converting vector embeddings into images to visualize their distribution
q: What does tokenization do in the NLP pipeline?

explain: Embeddings are dense vectors representing words or sentences: words with similar meaning have nearby vectors in the space.
options: Discrete labels of the BIO scheme assigned to tokens to mark named entities
Attention weight matrices with which the Transformer compares each token to the others
Dense vector representations that capture meaning and semantic relations between words
Numeric scores with which the BLEU metric evaluates the quality of automatic translations
q: What are embeddings in NLP?

explain: Models accept sequences up to a max sequence length: padding lengthens short sequences with special tokens and truncation cuts ones that are too long.
options: Increasing the tokenizer vocabulary size with additional new special tokens
Removing names and identifying data from clinical texts to anonymize patients
Computing precision and recall on predicted tokens to evaluate model quality
Making sequence lengths uniform to the max sequence length required by the model
q: What are padding and truncation for in preprocessing for Transformer models?

explain: Lowercasing, stopword and punctuation removal, and stemming/lemmatization are classic steps for cleaning and normalizing text before analysis.
options: Training a generative adversarial network (GAN) on texts to produce new synthetic content
Lowercasing and stopword removal: normalizing text to lowercase and eliminating common words
Raising the sampling temperature to make the model's generated responses more creative and varied
Quantizing the network weights by reducing their numeric precision to speed up inference
q: Which of the following is a typical NLP preprocessing operation?

explain: Extractive summarization copies existing sentences from the document; abstractive summarization generates new sentences that rephrase the content.
options: Translation and back-translation: converting text into another language and then translating it back
Binary and multi-label classification: assigning the document a single label or multiple labels together
Extractive and abstractive summarization: copying existing sentences or generating new ones
Tokenization and detokenization: splitting text into tokens and then reassembling it from tokens
q: One system summarizes by copying existing sentences from the document, another generates new sentences with its own words. What are the two approaches called?

explain: Machine translation automatically converts a text from a source language to a target language.
options: Machine translation: automatic conversion of a text from a source language to a target language
Named Entity Recognition: finding names of people, places, and organizations mentioned in text
Sentiment analysis: classifying the emotional polarity expressed in a text, e.g., positive or negative
Coreference resolution: linking pronouns and different mentions that refer to the same entity
q: Automatically converting a manual from Italian to English is a task of:

explain: SQuAD is the reference dataset for QA: over 100,000 questions asked on Wikipedia passages, with the answer contained in the passage.
options: An automatic metric for evaluating the quality of produced translations, such as the BLEU score
A neural model for automatic translation between different languages, such as an encoder-decoder Transformer
A subword tokenizer that splits rare words into frequent sub-units, such as BPE
A reference dataset for question answering, with questions asked on Wikipedia passages
q: What is SQuAD in the context of question answering?

explain: Accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions over the total evaluated examples.
options: TP divided by (TP + FP): fraction of entities predicted by the system that are truly correct
Fraction of correct predictions over the total evaluated examples
2 * precision * recall divided by (precision + recall): harmonic mean computed on the two measures
Overlap of n-grams between generated and reference text, as in the BLEU and ROUGE metrics
q: How is a classifier's accuracy computed?

explain: In open-domain QA there is no single given passage: a retriever searches a large knowledge base for relevant documents, then the reader/generator produces the answer.
options: Translating the question into English before searching the knowledge base for its answer
Computing the BLEU score of the generated answer by comparing it with a human reference
Retrieving the relevant passages from a large knowledge base to use for answering
Masking the named entities in the question to protect the end user's privacy
q: In an open-domain question answering system, what is the typical role of retrieval?

explain: Coreference resolution establishes which mentions (pronouns, names) refer to the same discourse entity.
options: Coreference resolution: linking mentions that refer to the same discourse entity
Sentiment analysis: classifying the emotional polarity expressed in the text, e.g., positive, negative, or neutral
Machine translation: automatically translating text from a source language to a target language
Tokenization: splitting text into minimal units such as words or subwords, mapped to numeric IDs
q: In the sentence 'Maria said that she will come tomorrow', understanding that 'she' refers to Maria is a task of:

explain: The first token of the entity takes B-LOC; subsequent tokens of the same entity take I-LOC.
options: B-LOC, B-LOC, B-LOC
B-LOC, I-LOC, I-LOC
I-LOC, I-LOC, I-LOC
O, O, O
q: In the sentence 'New York City is beautiful', if 'New York City' is a LOCATION entity, what is the correct BIO labeling?

explain: 'Barack' opens the person entity (B-PER), 'Obama' continues it (I-PER), common words are O, and 'Hawaii' opens the location (B-LOC).
options: B-PER, I-PER, O, O, O, B-LOC
I-PER, I-PER, O, O, O, I-LOC
B-PER, B-PER, O, O, O, B-LOC
B-PER, I-PER, O, O, O, I-LOC
q: In the sentence 'Barack Obama was born in Hawaii', with PERSON on 'Barack Obama' and LOCATION on 'Hawaii', what is the correct BIO sequence?

explain: NER finds names of people, places, and other identifiers, which can then be obscured or replaced to protect privacy.
options: Sentiment analysis on records to measure the emotional tone of clinical texts
Machine translation of records to translate them into another language before analysis
NER to find identifying data in texts, followed by anonymization
Abstractive summarization of records to generate short summaries of clinical cases
q: A hospital wants to automatically obscure patient names and places in clinical records before sharing them with researchers. Which solution is appropriate?

explain: Precision is TP/(TP+FP): among the entities predicted by the system, how many are truly correct.
options: TP / (TP + FN): fraction of all real entities that the system managed to find
(Precision + Recall) / 2: simple arithmetic mean computed on the two measures
TP / total tokens: number of correct entities divided by all tokens in the text
TP / (TP + FP): fraction of the entities predicted by the system that turn out correct
q: In NER evaluation, how is precision computed?

explain: Recall is TP/(TP+FN): among all real gold entities, how many the system managed to find.
options: TP / (TP + FP): fraction of the entities predicted by the system that turn out correct
TP / (TP + FN): fraction of all real entities that the system managed to find
2PR / (P + R): harmonic mean computed between precision and recall, i.e., the F1 measure
TN / (TP + FN): ratio of true negatives to real entities, a measure not used in NER
q: In NER evaluation, how is recall computed?

explain: High precision means few false positives; low recall means many false negatives, i.e., about half of the real entities are not found.
options: It finds almost all real entities but also produces a great many false alarms
Its F1 equals the arithmetic mean of 0.95 and 0.50, hence a score of 0.725
When it predicts an entity it is rarely wrong, but it misses about half of the real entities
It already has an F1 above 0.70, so no model improvement is needed
q: A NER system scores precision 0.95 and recall 0.50 on the test set. What does that mean?

explain: With imbalanced classes, accuracy is dominated by the majority class: a trivial model can look excellent without having learned anything, so precision, recall, and F1 are needed.
options: Accuracy is misleading: the model learns nothing; look at precision, recall, and F1
The model is excellent and ready for production, because 95% accuracy is outstanding
The dataset is too small to draw reliable conclusions about real performance
You only need to increase the max sequence length to give the classifier more context
q: A classifier on data with 95% negative examples scores 95% accuracy but always predicts the negative class. What is the correct conclusion?

explain: TF-IDF is a sparse bag-of-words statistic: it ignores order, context, and semantics, so 'not good' and 'good' share the term without negation; contextual BERT handles these phenomena.
options: It requires a GPU even for inference alone, while BERT never needs one
It does not handle numbers in texts and must always remove them during preprocessing
It works only on English texts and cannot be applied to texts in any other language
It ignores order, context, and semantics: it misses negation in sentences like 'not good'
q: What is the main limitation of TF-IDF with a classic classifier compared to a fine-tuned model like BERT?

explain: The standard architecture adds a linear layer with softmax on top of the representation of the special [CLS] token and retrains (fine-tuning) on the task's labeled data.
options: BERT's autoregressive decoder is used unchanged, generating the class name as free text
A classification head (linear layer + softmax) is added on the [CLS] token, with fine-tuning
A vocoder is connected to BERT's output to convert contextual embeddings into an audio signal
BERT's raw embeddings are used directly, with no additional training on the task
q: How is BERT typically used for a text classification task?

explain: Binary: two classes; multi-class: many mutually exclusive classes; multi-label: multiple labels applicable together to the same text.
options: Multi-label, multi-class, binary: first multiple labels together, then exclusive categories, then two classes
Multi-class, binary, multi-label: exclusive categories, then two classes, then multiple labels
Binary, multi-class, multi-label: only two classes, then exclusive categories, then multiple labels
Binary, multi-label, multi-class: two classes, then multiple labels, then exclusive categories
q: Reviews only positive/negative, tickets sorted into 50 exclusive categories, articles with multiple tags applied together: which settings do these correspond to, in order?

explain: Extractive QA does not generate text: it classifies each token as a possible answer start and end and returns the exact span of the passage.
options: It predicts the start and end indices (start/end) of the answer span inside the passage
It generates the answer token by token with an autoregressive decoder, as in generative QA
It translates the question and the passage into English before finding the correct answer
It groups passages with unsupervised clustering and picks the most likely cluster
q: How does an extractive question answering model like BERT trained on SQuAD work?

explain: Encoder-decoder and decoder-only models generate free-form answers token by token, even with words not present in the context.
options: Linear CRF: discriminative model for sequence labeling such as NER
TF-IDF + Naive Bayes: bag-of-words representation with a probabilistic classifier
SVM with kernel: maximum-margin classifier used with TF-IDF features
T5, BART, or GPT: generative models that produce the answer token by token
q: Which models are suited to generative (abstractive) question answering, which produces answers in its own words?

explain: SQuAD 2.0 adds about 50,000 unanswerable questions: the model must recognize when the passage does not contain the answer and abstain instead of inventing a span.
options: Only professional translations of the questions into other languages, to create a fully multilingual benchmark
Unanswerable questions: the model must know when to abstain
Only new questions asked on audio content automatically transcribed into text
Only new questions accompanied by images that the model must first describe in words
q: What does SQuAD 2.0 add over SQuAD 1.1?

explain: EM is binary and very strict: after normalization (lowercase, punctuation, articles) it is 1 only on perfect equality, so it is paired with F1, which rewards partial overlap.
options: The partial overlap between predicted and gold words, which also rewards merely incomplete answers
The ROUGE score of the generated summary computed against the human reference summary
1 if the prediction exactly matches a gold answer after normalization, 0 otherwise
The n-gram precision of the translation computed against the human reference, as in BLEU
q: What does Exact Match (EM) measure in question answering evaluation?

explain: It is the standard exam association: ROUGE (recall-oriented) for summarization, BLEU (precision with brevity penalty) for translation.
options: Summarization with ROUGE, translation with BLEU: content recall versus n-gram precision
Summarization with BLEU, translation with ROUGE: metrics swapped relative to standard use
NER with BLEU and QA with ROUGE: generation metrics applied to extractive tasks
Translation with accuracy and summarization with accuracy: simple fraction of outputs identical to the reference
q: What is the correct task-to-metric association?

explain: Text similarity measures how similar two texts are in meaning and is used for deduplication, FAQ matching, and ranking retrieved passages.
options: Named Entity Recognition: finding names of people, places, and organizations in text
Sentiment analysis: classifying the emotional polarity of the text as positive or negative
Machine translation: automatically translating text into another target language
Text similarity: measuring closeness of meaning between texts to deduplicate FAQs
q: Recognizing that 'How do I reset my password?' and 'I forgot my password, how do I set it again?' ask the same thing in order to deduplicate FAQs is a task of:

explain: Stemming mechanically cuts endings and can create non-existent fragments; lemmatization uses vocabulary and morphology to return the correct base form.
options: They are the same technique with different names: both always return the correct base form
Stemming truncates and can create non-words; lemmatization returns the correct base form
Stemming works only in English, while lemmatization applies to all other languages
Lemmatization always requires a neural network, while stemming uses rules and dictionaries
q: What is the difference between stemming and lemmatization?

explain: Word2Vec and GloVe assign a single vector per word, so different senses collapse; BERT's contextual embeddings change with the sentence and distinguish senses.
options: They are not vectors but discrete labels, one different label for each vocabulary word
They require more annotated data than BERT because they train only with full supervision on labeled sentences
They assign a single vector per word and do not distinguish different senses, such as those of 'bank'
They capture no semantic relation and assign completely random vectors to words
q: What is the limitation of static embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe compared to BERT's contextual embeddings?

explain: BPE and WordPiece split rare or unseen words into frequent sub-units already known to the vocabulary, effectively eliminating the out-of-vocabulary problem.
options: They split rare or unseen words into known sub-units of the existing vocabulary
They first translate each word into English and then apply the model's English vocabulary
They increase the max sequence length indefinitely, so even very long texts fit into the model
They replace learned embeddings with manual rules written by expert linguists
q: Why do subword tokenizers like BPE and WordPiece help with rare words or words never seen by the model?

explain: Macro-average averages the per-class metrics giving equal weight to each class; micro-average aggregates all examples and weighs frequent classes more.
options: They are two names for the same average and always produce the same value on every dataset
Macro is only for NER and micro only for QA: each applies to a single task
Micro ignores rare classes by removing them from the computation and evaluates only the most frequent classes
Macro gives equal weight to each class; micro aggregates examples and favors frequent classes
q: In a multi-class classification task, when does macro-average differ from micro-average, and why?

explain: Strict CoNLL evaluation requires exact boundaries and type: the partial span counts as a false positive and the missed gold entity as a false negative.
options: A true positive for both precision and recall, because the PERSON type is correct
A false positive and a false negative: both precision and recall are penalized
A true negative, because the system still found part of the correct entity
A case ignored by evaluation, because partial spans are never counted
q: The gold standard annotates 'Barack Obama' as PERSON, but the system predicts only 'Obama' as PERSON. In strict exact-match evaluation (CoNLL style), what happens?

explain: At token level, getting individual tokens right earns partial credit; at entity level, the entire chunk with correct boundaries and type is required, so it is stricter.
options: Token-level F1 gives partial credit; entity-level F1 requires the whole chunk to be correct
They are always identical by construction, because they use the same precision and recall formulas
Entity-level F1 is always higher, because it evaluates larger informative units
Token-level F1 cannot use the BIO scheme and requires different labels
q: What is the difference between token-level F1 and entity-level F1 in NER evaluation?

explain: F1 = 2*P*R/(P+R) = 2*0.8*0.4/1.2 = 0.64/1.2 = approx. 0.53. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the lower value, unlike the arithmetic mean (0.60).
options: 0.60 - arithmetic mean of precision and recall, the typical mistake of those using the simple mean
0.32 - product of precision and recall, without the harmonic mean of the F1 formula
0.53 - harmonic mean 2*P*R/(P+R), pulled toward the lower value
0.80 - equal to precision, as if recall did not count in the F1 computation
q: A classifier has precision 0.8 and recall 0.4. What is the F1 score?

explain: The shared word is one out of one predicted (precision 1.0) and one out of two gold (recall 0.5), so F1 = 2*1*0.5/1.5 = approx. 0.67; EM is 0 because the strings do not match exactly.
options: F1 = 1.0 and EM = 1: answer considered perfectly identical to gold
F1 = 0.5 and EM = 1: EM assigned although the strings differ
F1 = 0.75 and EM = 0: arithmetic mean of precision and recall instead of the harmonic mean
F1 approx. 0.67 and EM = 0: one shared word out of one predicted and one out of two gold
q: In QA the gold answer is 'Paris, France' and the model predicts 'Paris'. What are the token-level F1 and Exact Match?

explain: BLEU measures n-gram precision: without a penalty, emitting a few safe words would suffice; the brevity penalty lowers the score of translations that are too short relative to the reference.
options: It rewards long translations regardless of quality, without applying any penalty
It penalizes translations that are too short with few safe words; BLEU is precision-oriented
It measures the recall of extractive summaries, i.e., how much of the reference is covered
It replaces human evaluation in all cases, making manual judgments unnecessary
q: What is the brevity penalty in BLEU for, and how does it differ from ROUGE?

explain: ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence between the generated summary and the reference: it captures content coverage and word order without requiring rigid consecutive matches like ROUGE-2.
options: The overlap of single unigrams between the generated summary and the human reference summary
The overlap of consecutive bigrams between the generated summary and the human reference
The longest common subsequence between generated and reference: word coverage and order
The brevity penalty of translations, which punishes outputs that are too short in BLEU
q: What does ROUGE-L measure in summarization evaluation?

explain: Natural Questions collects real questions asked to Google with answers annotated on Wikipedia; MS MARCO collects Bing questions with generated answers and relevance judgments, also designed for passage ranking.
options: NQ uses real Google questions on Wikipedia; MS MARCO uses Bing questions with relevance judgments
They are two different names for the same identical SQuAD dataset, used interchangeably in the literature
MS MARCO evaluates only automatic translation between English and other world languages
Natural Questions evaluates only NER, i.e., recognizing people and places in texts
q: What is the difference between the Natural Questions and MS MARCO datasets for question answering?

explain: NER extracts mentions from unstructured text; entity linking and relation extraction connect them into knowledge graph nodes and edges.
options: Only sentiment analysis on articles to measure the positive or negative tone of texts
Only automatic translation of articles into English before indexing them in the graph
Only extractive summarization to copy the most important sentences of each article
NER to extract entities, plus entity linking and relations to connect them in the graph
q: A publisher wants to build a knowledge graph from thousands of articles (people, companies, places, and their relations). Which NLP pipeline fits?

explain: With a few dozen examples for many classes, training from scratch is impractical; LLMs classify well in zero/few-shot or via embeddings without updating weights, as also required by the NCA-GENL blueprint.
options: Training an LSTM network fully from scratch using only the five examples of each category
Writing fully hand-crafted regex rules, one different rule for each category
Zero/few-shot prompting or classification via embeddings, without heavy training
Applying K-means to the individual characters of tickets to group them without supervision
q: You must sort tickets into 50 categories with only 5 examples each and no large annotated datasets. What is the best approach?

explain: High precision says the few entities found are right; recall 0.45 says over half of the entities are missed, so the priority is broadening coverage (data, gazetteers, thresholds) without destroying precision.
options: Raising the confidence threshold to further increase the NER system's precision
Changing the evaluation metric and using BLEU instead of precision, recall, and F1
Collecting much more test data without touching the model, to better measure performance
Working on recall: more annotated data, gazetteers, and thresholds, without destroying precision
q: A production NER system has entity precision 0.90 but recall 0.45 on the test set. What is the priority intervention?

explain: Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 if they point in the same semantic direction, and it is the standard metric for comparing text embeddings.
options: The edit distance between strings, i.e., the number of insertions and deletions
The cosine of the angle between the vectors: close to 1 indicates very similar meanings
The count of words shared between documents divided by the total length
The probability estimated by a classifier that two texts have the same author
q: What does cosine similarity between two text embeddings measure?

explain: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: the system retrieves relevant passages from a knowledge base and passes them to the model as context to generate the answer.
options: A pruning and quantization technique that compresses the weights of the trained model
A training run that updates all model parameters on new labeled data
The retrieval of relevant passages used as context to generate the answer
An unsupervised clustering that groups documents by homogeneous topic
q: What does the acronym RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) mean?

explain: FAISS is Meta's open-source library for efficient similarity search over dense vectors, with approximate search (ANN) indexes suited to millions of embeddings.
options: A generative Meta model for extractive-type question answering
A relational database with distributed SQL transactions and complex joins
A subword tokenizer that splits rare words into known frequent units
An open-source Meta library for fast search among similar vectors
q: What is FAISS in the context of RAG systems?

explain: Top-k retrieval selects the k chunks with the highest similarity score to the question and passes them to the model as context; typical values are k = 3-5.
options: Training the model for k epochs on the indexed company documents
Selecting the k passages most similar to the question to use as context
Using k GPUs in parallel to speed up answer generation
Generating k alternative answers from which the user picks the best
q: In a RAG pipeline, what does the expression top-k retrieval refer to?

explain: With frequently changing documents, RAG updates the knowledge base without retraining anything: just re-index the new manuals and the model uses them right away.
options: A full fine-tuning repeated every week on all model weights
Prompt engineering with a few fixed instructions written once and for all
A RAG system that indexes the manuals and reuses them as updated context
An automatic translation of the manuals with no search mechanism
q: A company has manuals that change every week and wants up-to-date answers without retraining the model. Which solution fits?

explain: LangChain is a framework that provides composable components (splitters, embeddings, vector stores, retrievers, chains) for building LLM applications such as RAG systems.
options: An embedding model for multilingual text trained on parallel sentence pairs
A distributed vector database alternative to solutions like Milvus and Pinecone
An evaluation metric that measures the faithfulness of generated RAG answers
A framework of composable components for building LLM-based applications
q: What is LangChain in the context of RAG applications?

explain: Cosine of 1 means vectors in the same direction (maximum similarity), 0 means orthogonal vectors (no similarity), -1 opposite direction.
options: 1 means maximum similarity, 0 no similarity, and -1 opposite direction
0 means maximum similarity, 1 no similarity, and -1 a computation error
Values range from 0 to 100 and above 50 similarity is considered perfect
-1 means maximum similarity, 1 no similarity, and 0 a null vector
q: How do you interpret cosine similarity values between two embeddings?

explain: Since the answer is generated from retrieved passages, the system can cite the sources used, making the answer verifiable, unlike purely parametric generation.
options: The model generates more creative answers by raising the sampling temperature
The system cites the source documents, so the answer stays verifiable
The model removes the context window and accepts infinitely long documents
The system no longer requires any document in the external knowledge base
q: What advantage does RAG offer over an LLM used without retrieval, from a verifiability standpoint?

explain: The embedding model converts texts into dense vectors that capture meaning: it is the component that makes semantic search possible in a RAG system.
options: Evaluating with BLEU scores the quality of the translations produced by the system
Assigning BIO labels to the named entities in the indexed documents
Generating the final answer token by token with an autoregressive decoder
Converting texts into dense vectors that capture meaning for search
q: What is the role of an embedding model inside a RAG system?

explain: Chunks that are too large include irrelevant text and waste context window; chunks that are too small lose the context needed to understand the passage, so a compromise is needed.
options: Size never matters: only the number of indexed documents counts
Small chunks are always better because the model reads them faster
Large chunks add noise and waste context; small chunks lose it
Large chunks eliminate hallucinations; small chunks always increase them
q: What is the trade-off in choosing chunk size in a RAG system?

explain: Hybrid search combines dense search (embeddings, meaning) and sparse search (BM25, exact words such as codes and proper names), combining the scores for a more robust ranking.
options: Using two different LLMs in parallel to generate the same identical answer
Joint training on texts and images for multimodal-type answers
Combining CPU and GPU during the vector indexing phase
Fusing dense search over embeddings and sparse search like BM25
q: What is hybrid search in advanced RAG systems?

explain: Fine-tuning changes the weights to durably change the model's behavior, style, and skills; RAG instead adds external knowledge without touching the weights.
options: When documents change every day and always up-to-date knowledge is needed
When the exact sources of the company private documents used must be cited
When the model's style, tone, and behavior must be changed durably
When there is no external document to index in the system
q: In which case is fine-tuning preferable to RAG?

explain: Hallucinations arise from purely parametric generation; RAG grounds the answer in real documents supplied in the context, reducing invented claims.
options: By grounding generation in real documents provided in the answer's context
By raising the temperature to make answers more varied and more creative
By removing retrieved documents and answering only from parametric memory
By disabling retrieval and shortening the model's context window
q: How does RAG help reduce model hallucinations?

explain: With unit-norm normalized vectors, sorting by Euclidean distance or by cosine similarity gives the same ranking, because the two measures become monotonically linked.
options: Euclidean distance applies only to English; cosine to all languages
Cosine requires sparse vectors while Euclidean requires dense vectors
Euclidean distance is always more accurate than cosine on any embedding
With normalized vectors the two measures give the same final ranking
q: What is the relation between Euclidean (L2) distance and cosine similarity when embeddings are normalized?

explain: The retriever abstracts search: given the question, it queries the vector store and returns the most relevant chunks, which the chain then inserts into the model's prompt.
options: Querying the vector store with the question and passing useful chunks to the chain
Retraining the model weights on every new question asked by the end user
Converting the generated answer into an audio file with an external voice model
Encrypting private documents before saving them in the company vector database
q: What is the role of a retriever in a LangChain application?

explain: Sentence embeddings represent whole sentences as single vectors optimized for semantic similarity, while Word2Vec assigns a static vector to each word with no sentence-level context.
options: Sentence embeddings are discrete labels; Word2Vec produces continuous vectors
Word2Vec works only in English; sentence embeddings only in Italian
Sentence embeddings encode sentences for similarity; Word2Vec gives static vectors
There is no difference: they are two names for the same identical neural model
q: What is the difference between sentence embeddings and Word2Vec for semantic retrieval?

explain: The bi-encoder encodes question and documents separately for fast large-scale search; the cross-encoder processes them together for a more accurate relevance score, typical of re-ranking.
options: Bi-encoder encodes them separately for fast search; cross-encoder together for re-ranking
Bi-encoder generates free text with the decoder; cross-encoder only images and audio
The cross-encoder is always faster and replaces the bi-encoder in every stage
